tags.gist: Says the supervised-versus-autonomous distinction on the activity axis cannot be verified from audit records, which hold one actor per event and so hide drift.
Wants attribution traceability, whether records separate authenticating, acting and authorizing identities, as a framework dimension raising risk when absent.
Notes a thorough public reference implementation still cannot yield a record from which supervision is recoverable, since its trace sits in platform telemetry.
Says the HL7 audit extension cannot express an agent acting for another agent, so supervisory-agent records could not name the accountable clinician.
Suggests testable criteria: attribution emitted not inferred, unattributed agent actions positively recorded, and attribution strength stated.
Says the standards gap has an owner and open process, and an FDA expectation about what records preserve would move it faster than new rules.
Argues a device authorized as supervised that later runs unsupervised produces records identical to the supervised case, so the drift is unrepresented.
Frames attribution traceability as a risk dimension, a precondition for supervisory agents and a testable agentic acceptance criterion.
Separates authenticating, acting and authorizing identities and wants devices whose records cannot preserve that distinction placed at higher risk.
Describes a careful twelve-agent prototype whose agent participation survives only in vendor telemetry, so clinician-composed and agent-drafted records look alike.
Prefers attribution held as scalar metadata within the audit record rather than retained prompts, which create a disclosure surface over real patients.
Details why the draft HL7 on-behalf-of extension excludes devices and misroutes requestor queries, asking FDA to check records can express supervision before relying on supervisors.
Wants oversight-checkpoint compliance recorded in production, with emitted attribution, positively marked unattributed actions and stated attribution strength as acceptance criteria.
Assigns standards bodies the definition of attribution semantics, keeping manufacturers accountable for what devices emit and helping small providers inherit the capability.
Names a fourth change type, erosion of human involvement without any software change, which degradation monitoring can only see if records distinguish authorized actions.
Limits its claims: attribution cannot detect a non-cooperating agent, is offered within existing criteria rather than as new burden, and its artifacts are not devices.
